This is possibly a "friends don't let friends" kind of thing

Still, let's see where this takes us:

```{r}
#| error: true
#| eval: false
#| output: false

head(penguins_raw)
pen_id <- c(1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6)
pen_species <- c("Adelie", "Adelie", "Adelie", "Adelie")

diy_penguins <- data.frame(
  id = pen_id,
  species = pen_species
)
cbind(pen_id, pen_species)

pen_species <- rep("Adelie", 6)
diy_penguins <- data.frame(
  id = pen_id,
  species = pen_species
)
diy_penguins
cbind(pen_id, pen_species)
```

# I/O: Data in

## Data in

Data can come in different formats (and shapes, possibly):

::: {.fragment}
- Your files, the clipboard, a URL
- Plain text file: Comma-separated, tab-delimited, ...
- R format file
- SAS/Stata/SPSS file (there's the CRAN package `haven`)
- Spreadsheet (Excel) - package `readxl` is highly recommended!
- Database: RSQLite, RPostgreSQL, RMySQL, ...
:::

::: {.fragment}
Colleagues might even provide data to you as a/within a package (I did that a long time ago -  see https://github.com/federicomarini/rbioc2016 for an example)

R is a language, we need to learn the words that do things. 
:::

## The vocabulary of importing

... and exporting

- `read.table()`,`write.table()` + `read.csv()`, `read.delim()`
- `load()`,`save()`/`readRDS()`,`saveRDS()`
- via `haven` : `read_sas()`,`read_spss()` /`write_sas()`,`write_sav()`
- via `readxl`: `read_excel()`

::: {.fragment}
Check out their documentation pages!

Other options: `vroom::vroom()`, the RStudio GUI, ...

Who has seen the option `stringsAsFactors=FALSE`?
:::

# On pain, paths, files, and projects

## Where is R right now?

```{r}
#| eval: false
getwd()
list.files()
```

::: {.fragment}
- R always works **from one folder**: the *working directory*
- Every file you name is looked for **relative to that folder**
- Check the **Files pane**: it shows the same folder
:::

## Absolute vs. relative paths

```{r}
#| eval: false
# absolute: works on ONE computer only
read_csv("C:/Users/maria/Desktop/course/datasets/nhanes.csv")

# relative: works on ANY computer that has the same project
read_csv("datasets/nhanes.csv")
```

::: {.fragment}
An absolute path in your code means nobody else can run it, and neither can *future you* on a new laptop.

Use RStudio projects -> Opening the project **sets the working directory to that folder**, and everything lives together: `.qmd`, `datasets/`, outputs

Rule/suggestion: one project per analysis, and refer to files relative to it
:::

::: {.fragment}
### Typical path errors

* `cannot open file ... No such file` --> typo, wrong folder, or project not opened 
* `'C:\Users\...' contains an unrecognized escape` --> Windows backslashes: use `/` 
:::

## Quarto and the working directory

Works in the console, fails on render?

When you **render** a `.qmd`, the working directory is **the folder of the document**.

::: {.fragment}
Keep the `.qmd` in the project root, and relative paths just work

My heartfelt tip: Never-ever-ever  use `setwd()` in a document. It hard-codes your machine into the analysis.
:::

## Working with a vector

```{r}
my_first_vec <- c(6, 1, 3, 6, 10, 5)
```

::: {.fragment}
What happens if you do this?

```{r}
#| eval: false

my_first_vec[2]
my_first_vec[c(5, 6)]
my_first_vec[-c(5,6)]
my_first_vec > 5
my_first_vec[my_first_vec > 5]
```
:::

## How to access what is in a data frame?

Slicing and dicing, the basic way - most rectangular datasets can be dealt with...

```{r eval=FALSE}
dataset[ROWS, COLUMNS]
```

You can subset with...

::: {.fragment}
- integers
- blank spaces
- names
- logical vectors
:::

::: {.fragment}
Sometimes you could think it's all about the money (`$`)

## Grooming them well

Let's return back to the `penguins_raw`

::: {.fragment}
```{r}
#| results: false
my_penguins <- penguins_raw

my_penguins$`Sample Number`
my_penguins$Sex
my_penguins$Species
```
:::

::: {.fragment}
Everything (well, almost) is a character!

Which ones of these should NOT be text
:::

::: {.fragment}
* Sample number is a number - but it is not
* Sex and Species are actually categories - factors come into play
* Date Egg is a date - and you might encounter them often in epidemiological datasets
:::

## Grooming - Round 2

Column names have those nasty spaces...

::: {.fragment}
```{r}
#| results: false
library("janitor")
my_penguins <- my_penguins |> clean_names()

colnames(penguins_raw)
colnames(my_penguins)
```
:::

::: {.fragment}
Can you also make the `species` information more compact?

How can we drop the comments?
:::

::: {.fragment}
```{r}
my_penguins <- my_penguins[, -17]
my_penguins$comments <- NULL
```
:::

## Transforming penguins

Let's work on the body mass

* Make it in kilograms
* Compute a Z score out of it (challenge: do it by hand!)
  * How can you check if this is somehow normally distributed?
* Categorize that in some classes

::: {.fragment}
```{r}
#| results: false
#| fig-show: hide
my_penguins$mass_kg <- my_penguins$body_mass_g / 1000

hist(my_penguins$body_mass_g, breaks = 20)

my_penguins$z_mass <- as.numeric(scale(my_penguins$body_mass_g))
hist(my_penguins$z_mass, breaks = 20)

my_penguins$mass_class <- cut(my_penguins$body_mass_g, breaks = 4)
```
:::

::: {.fragment}
What if you want to specify those limits by hand? 
<!-- assist to use mutate -->
:::

## Transforming penguins, with `dplyr`

::: {.fragment}
```{r}
library("dplyr")
my_penguins$body_mass_g |> summary()

my_penguins |> 
  mutate(mc2 = case_when(
    body_mass_g < 3500 ~ "light",
    body_mass_g < 4500 ~ "medium",
    .default = "heavy")
  ) -> my_penguins

table(my_penguins$mc2)
```
:::

::: {.fragment}
Notice here the "right hand assignment" & the order of the classes - what "should be done on top"?
:::

# I/O: Data out

## We are done for the day

Let's save/export things - there are many ways to do so

::: {.fragment}
```{r}
#| eval: true
#| results: hide

head(my_penguins)
dir.create("output")

save(my_penguins, file = "output/mypeng.RData")
saveRDS(my_penguins, file = "output/mypeng.RDS")

write.csv(my_penguins, file = "output/my_penguins.csv")
write.csv(my_penguins, file = "output/my_penguins_norownames.csv", row.names = FALSE)
readr::write_csv(my_penguins, file = "output/my_penguins_with_readr.csv")
write.table(my_penguins, file = "output/my_penguins.txt", sep = ";")

writexl::write_xlsx(my_penguins, path = "output/my_penguins.xlsx")

save.image(file = "output/my_session.RData")
```
:::

::: {.fragment}
CHECK - THOSE - OPTIONS (or get burned afterwards...)

Options worth checking: `quote`, `na`, `col.names`, ...
:::

## Some extra challenges

* Take your first analytical decision: remove some data points, e.g. filter out the rows where we have no info on the sex
* Clean up the text values (species, for example)
* (harder) Make your `my_penguins` look like as similar as possible to the `penguins`
* (harder) This dataset is in the so-called wide format, and it has FOUR essential measurements - can you think of a way to make it in the long format? "How can this be useful"? (the `tidyr` package can be your friend!)
* Excel files can be a real mess - can you find one out in the wild and import that?

```{r}
#| eval: false
#| echo: false

library("tidyr")

# 1. Wide -> long -----------------------------------------------
peng_long <- penguins |>
  mutate(id = row_number()) |>
  select(id, species, sex,
         bill_len, bill_dep, flipper_len, body_mass) |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols      = c(bill_len, bill_dep, flipper_len, body_mass),
    names_to  = "measurement",
    values_to = "value"
  )

# Predict first: how many rows should this have?
nrow(penguins) * 4
nrow(peng_long)

# 2. Payoff: one plot, all four measurements ---------------------
library("ggplot2")
ggplot(peng_long, aes(x = species, y = value)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  facet_wrap(~ measurement, scales = "free_y")

ggplot(peng_long, aes(x = species, y = value)) +
  ggforce::geom_sina() +
  facet_wrap(~ measurement, scales = "free_y")

# 3. Long -> wide: a cross-tab ----------------------------------
penguins |>
  count(species, island)

penguins |>
  count(species, island) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = island, values_from = n, values_fill = 0)

# 4. Round trip: back to the original shape ----------------------
peng_back <- peng_long |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = measurement, values_from = value)

dim(peng_back)   # same number of rows as penguins?
```
